beanstalk.name: AWS Elastic Beanstalk
beanstalk.role: Deploy an application; let Beanstalk coordinate its infrastructure.
bullets: Standard environments manage EC2, load balancing, scaling, deployment and health.
Use .ebextensions/<name>.config (YAML/JSON) for environment options, instance customization and extra CloudFormation resources.
Environment-created resources normally share its lifecycle; keep durable RDS outside it. A disposable session cache can be recreated.
beanstalk.boundary: Rolling can reduce serving capacity and leave mixed versions after failure. Immutable/traffic splitting replace the fleet and lose accumulated CPU burst credits. Blue/green uses separate environments and a CNAME swap.
beanstalk.example:
option_settings:
  aws:elasticbeanstalk:command:
    DeploymentPolicy: RollingWithAdditionalBatch
    BatchSizeType: Fixed
    BatchSize: 2

# Install a tool on the environment's EC2 instances.
packages:
  yum:
    jq: []

# Provision a managed cache in the environment stack.
Resources:
  SessionCache:
    Type: AWS::ElastiCache::CacheCluster
    Properties:
      Engine: memcached
      CacheNodeType: cache.t3.micro
      NumCacheNodes: 1
      CacheSubnetGroupName: example-cache-subnets
      VpcSecurityGroupIds:
        - sg-0123456789abcdef0

rows: May drop to zero; quickest rollout
Reduced by the batch being updated
Keep old fleet intact while validating new

beanstalk.note: Replace the cache subnet group/security group placeholders with compatible existing VPC resources and allow application access to the cache. This excerpt omits network setup; it has no retention policy, so the cache follows environment deletion. On a failed rolling deployment, replacement instances use the last successful app version; redeploy to restore consistency.

learning.title: Managed environment, underlying CloudFormation
paragraphs: Elastic Beanstalk uses CloudFormation to launch environment resources, then manages deployments, health and scaling. An .ebextensions Resources definition extends that environment stack; disposal/retention rules still matter.

Inspect Beanstalk events and underlying stack events for provisioning failures. Avoid uncoordinated manual changes to managed resources. A failed immutable rollout and a failed in-place rolling rollout have different rollback/isolation boundaries.
learning.trap: Environment-managed infrastructure is not proof that every custom script-created external resource is tracked or safely retained.

learning.title: Worker tier: scheduled jobs use cron.yaml and SQS
paragraphs: **Web server** environments handle user HTTP requests; **worker** environments process background jobs from SQS. A leader scheduler uses cron.yaml in the application source bundle to enqueue recurring work. The worker daemon polls SQS and POSTs to the application’s local HTTP endpoint; a successful response lets it delete the message.

**.ebextensions/*.config** customises environment resources/configuration. **cron.yaml** is the native recurring worker-task mechanism. OS cron can be installed/configured separately, but is not the same scheduling path. Jobs must tolerate retries and duplicate delivery.
learning.analogy: The timetable creates a work ticket; SQS holds tickets until a worker calls the back-office endpoint.

rows: Handles requests through the web tier
Daemon forwards message body to local app endpoint

learning.example:
# cron.yaml at source-bundle root; worker tier
version: 1
cron:
  - name: "process-videos"
    url: "/process-videos"
    schedule: "0 * * * *"
# Scheduler → SQS → daemon → POST /process-videos (hourly).
learning.trigger: Native scheduled Beanstalk background task → worker tier + cron.yaml, not a web-tier cron file.
learning.trap: A schedule enqueues work; it does not guarantee exact execution time or exactly-once side effects.

ec2.name: Amazon EC2
ec2.role: A virtual machine with OS and instance-level control.
bullets: Linux user-data shell scripts run as root, normally on the first launch boot only. Configure cloud-init explicitly for later boots.
Stop an EBS-backed instance before changing its user-data attribute; changing it does not itself rerun the script.
T-family instances spend CPU credits on bursts; sustained CPU demand needs an appropriate family or credit configuration.
ec2.boundary: Hardware isolation alone points to Dedicated Instances; physical host placement or socket/core licensing points to Dedicated Hosts.
ec2.example:
#!/bin/bash
# Amazon Linux example; first-boot setup, not a recurring job.
dnf install -y nginx
systemctl enable --now nginx

docs.label: Current vs legacy EC2 Free Tier

rows: Dedicated customer hardware; no host placement

learning.title: Regional vs Zonal Reserved Instances

rows: Matching usage discount across AZs in a Region; eligible instance-size flexibility
Matching discount + capacity reserved in one specified AZ
Must match reservation attributes; capacity availability subject to purchase; not multi-AZ HA
Reserve matching EC2 capacity in a chosen AZ independently of RI commitment
Billing discounts and capacity guarantees are separate decisions

learning.trigger: Need matching EC2 capacity in a particular AZ → a Zonal RI or an appropriate On-Demand Capacity Reservation; Regional RI alone is insufficient.

learning.title: gp2 vs gp3, and what EC2 monitoring sees
paragraphs: **gp2:** baseline 3 IOPS/GiB, minimum 100 and maximum 16,000 IOPS; small volumes can burst using credits. A 100 GiB volume has 300 baseline IOPS, not a permanent 3,000 IOPS guarantee.

**gp3:** performance is provisioned independently of size, with a 3,000 IOPS / 125 MiB/s baseline; current general-purpose volume limits reach **80,000 IOPS / 2,000 MiB/s** subject to volume size/IOPS ratios and the EC2 platform’s EBS bandwidth. Outposts has lower limits. Unlike gp2, gp3 does not use burst credits.

EC2 basic monitoring publishes most metrics every **5 minutes**; detailed monitoring publishes them every **1 minute**. NetworkOut is native. Guest RAM usage and filesystem/disk-space utilisation need the CloudWatch agent/custom metrics; native disk I/O metrics are not free-space utilisation.
learning.trap: Detailed monitoring changes frequency, not the set of guest memory/filesystem metrics.

learning.title: Replacement cutover: stable IP vs DNS redundancy
paragraphs: An **Elastic IP** is a static public IPv4 address allocated in one Region. Prepare/test instance B while A serves, then reassociate the EIP to B. Clients keep the address, but reassociation and connection recovery can briefly interrupt traffic; this is not guaranteed zero-downtime.

For a self-hosted authoritative DNS service that must keep its EC2 public IP, EIP reassociation can meet the address constraint. Route 53 DNS failover changes routing answers and has detection, TTL and resolver-cache effects; it does not automatically preserve that instance’s address. Independent authoritative nameservers improve resilience beyond one server.
learning.analogy: Keep the published phone number while moving it to a prepared office; some calls can drop during the transfer.

rows: Longer no-ready-server gap; auto public address may change
Same public IPv4; brief cutover interruption possible
Redundancy; detection/caching affect failover; multiple addresses
More infrastructure, health and DNS design

learning.trigger: Must preserve an EC2-hosted service’s public IPv4 while replacing the instance → consider EIP reassociation within its Region.
learning.trap: Immutable replacement means a new deployment target; it does not itself guarantee continuous service or automatically move an EIP.

asg.name: EC2 Auto Scaling
asg.role: Maintain fleet capacity across AZs; pair with ELB to route traffic.
bullets: One ASG belongs to one Region and uses subnets in one or more AZs. It normally attempts to balance instances across enabled AZs.
The group replaces unhealthy instances and scales instance count in/out. Changing instance size is a separate vertical-scaling operation.
ELB distributes requests across registered targets. Its cross-zone setting controls whether an LB node can route outside its own AZ; it does not rebalance the instance fleet.
asg.boundary: Cross-zone ≠ cross-Region. An ASG and a regional load balancer stay within one Region. Use separate regional stacks plus Route 53 or Global Accelerator for global traffic routing.
asg.note: DesiredCapacity=10 sets the fleet total, not a 2/8 AZ allocation. A launch template supplies AMI, instance type, security groups and bootstrap configuration. Scale against the measured bottleneck.

lab.label: Try min / max / desired / current capacity

learning.title: Which metric should drive target tracking?
paragraphs: Predefined metrics include ASGAverageCPUUtilization, ASGAverageNetworkIn, ASGAverageNetworkOut and ALBRequestCountPerTarget (with the target-group/load-balancer resource label). Pick a metric that changes appropriately as worker capacity changes.

EC2 **NetworkOut** counts bytes sent by the instance; ASGAverageNetworkOut is an aggregate target-tracking choice. SQS queue depth alone does not normalise for workers: use a custom/metric-math **visible backlog per InService instance**.

Target backlog per worker = acceptable delay / average processing time. With 60 s acceptable delay and 2 s/message, target 30 visible messages/worker. Handle zero workers explicitly; adding workers cannot fix a downstream bottleneck.
learning.trigger: Scale consumers from queue demand → backlog per worker, not CPU by default.
learning.trap: ASG maintains capacity across configured AZs in one Region. It does not route requests or create multi-Region failover.

alb.name: Application Load Balancer
alb.role: Route HTTP requests to healthy targets.
bullets: An internet-facing ALB routes HTTP requests to healthy targets, including targets with private IP addresses.
Health checks have their own path, port, matcher and network reachability; direct access can work while a target is unhealthy.
With cross-zone balancing and equal healthy target weights, 2 targets in AZ A + 8 in AZ B means about 10% per target.
alb.boundary: ALB access logs describe requests. CloudWatch metrics aggregate measurements. CloudTrail describes AWS API/account activity.

rows: Which client, URL, status and target timing?
Request details; not the application body or a complete audit ledger
Who changed a listener or security setting?
Administrative AWS API activity; not each HTTP request
Check path, port, matcher, security groups and NACLs

alb.note: Request tracing supplies an X-Amzn-Trace-Id for correlation; instrumentation is still needed for downstream spans. The 10% example assumes request-count routing, not differing target weights, stickiness or connection behaviour.

learning.title: Host/path rules, stickiness and uneven traffic
paragraphs: `smart.com/api` selects a **path-pattern** rule such as `/api*`; `api.smart.com` selects a **host-header** rule. They can also be combined. An ALB listener routes to a target group; its algorithm, healthy targets and connections determine the observed distribution.

ALB cross-zone is always enabled at load-balancer level, but can be disabled for supported target groups. Sticky sessions bind a client session to a target and can skew counts; they require cross-zone enabled. Unequal instance types do not automatically receive traffic in proportion to CPU/RAM.

Legacy **Classic Load Balancer** supports basic listener/backend routing, cookie stickiness and cross-zone settings, but lacks ALB host/path target-group rules. CLB uses round robin for TCP listeners and least outstanding requests for HTTP/HTTPS; ALB supports configurable target-group algorithms. Unequal instance types do not create automatic CPU-proportional target weights.
learning.trigger: Same hostname, different URL paths → ALB path rules; different subdomains → host rules.
learning.trap: 2+8 targets → about 10% each is an idealised equal-weight example, not a guarantee of exactly equal request counts.

learning.title: Listener → rule → target group → target
paragraphs: An ALB belongs to **one Region and VPC**. An internet-facing ALB has public-facing endpoints; an internal ALB requires private connectivity. Both can forward to private backends. Listeners accept configured HTTP/HTTPS ports; listener rules choose a target group.

A host rule matches the HTTP Host header; it does not make “hostname” a target type. IP registration does not create peering, routes, security-group permissions, NACL rules or return paths. Reachable private IPs outside the VPC can be supported targets; publicly routable IPs cannot be registered as IP targets.
learning.analogy: The public reception desk selects a department; the department’s target list gives the actual office address. A name on the list does not build a road there.
learning.flow: Client → ALB DNS endpoint → HTTPS listener :443 → host/path rule → target group → healthy backend.

rows: Primary private IP of primary EC2 network interface
Register instance IDs in the ALB VPC
Same VPC or reachable supported private network; no public IP targets
Function permission; not a target-subnet TCP connection

learning.trigger: Public frontend + private backend is normal. Other-VPC private IP → verify actual forward/return connectivity.
learning.trap: Host-based routing is a listener rule, not a target type. Registration alone does not guarantee health or reachability.

apigw.name: Amazon API Gateway
apigw.role: Expose an API with routing, integration and access controls.
bullets: A stage is a named environment pointing to an API deployment snapshot. A canary tests a newer deployment on the same stage URL.
Stage variables configure integrations; VTL mapping templates transform payloads. A proxy integration instead passes its standard event to the backend.
Authorizers establish caller access. Usage plans meter API-key consumers; caching can avoid repeated backend work.
apigw.boundary: API keys are not authentication. Usage-plan quotas/throttles are best effort, not hard spend limits. Verify the API type before selecting a feature.
apigw.exampleTitle: Control-plane example · create a usage plan (API request body)
apigw.note: Create or import PartnerApp’s API key, then attach it to this plan separately. Mark GET /GetOrder as API Key Required. Both stages share this example’s per-key limits; the key does not route traffic. Quotas/throttles are best effort. Cache only safely scoped responses, with TTL/invalidation appropriate for changes in data and entitlements.

learning.title: REST API integration types — MOCK has no backend

rows: API Gateway creates response from configured mappings/responses
Contract tests/stubs; no Lambda/HTTP backend invoked
Lambda proxy event → Lambda; function returns proxy response
No custom VTL body transformation contract
AWS service or Lambda custom integration
Forward to HTTP endpoint with proxy behaviour
Mapping templates/response mappings can transform payloads

learning.trigger: Return a test response without calling any backend → MOCK.
learning.trap: API Gateway API type matters: this is the REST API integration vocabulary; HTTP APIs have a different feature/API model.

learning.title: HTTP anatomy and authorised cache refresh
paragraphs: With caching enabled, an appropriately authorised `Cache-Control: max-age=0` request fetches a fresh integration response and updates that entry. Configure the method to require authorisation and grant **execute-api:InvalidateCache** to the caller. For unauthorised invalidation, configuration can return **403**, ignore with a response warning, or ignore silently. Cross-account cache invalidation is not supported.

An unexpired cached response may still be stale relative to the source data. Expired/missing entries fetch from the backend normally. Cache keys must distinguish the response inputs and authorised data scope.
learning.analogy: A waiter can reuse an unexpired order slip; an authorised “check again” instruction asks the kitchen for a fresh answer.
learning.flow: GET /prod/GetOrder?id=42 → stage/method → cache key → cached response or backend → cache update.

rows: Request parameter; include relevant values in cache key
Payload; not a replacement for a header

learning.example:
# Executable curl shape; add configured authentication/signing as needed
curl -H "Cache-Control: max-age=0" \
  "https://API_ID.execute-api.ap-southeast-2.amazonaws.com/prod/GetOrder?id=42"
# Header alone does not grant execute-api:InvalidateCache.
learning.trigger: Refresh a REST API cached entry → Cache-Control: max-age=0 plus required permission/configuration.
learning.trap: ?bypass_cache=1 and Bypass-Cache: 1 have no built-in invalidation meaning. HTTP APIs do not offer the same REST managed response cache.

learning.title: Stage configuration vs three permission directions
paragraphs: A REST stage references a deployed API snapshot. Stage variables are stage-owned key/value configuration, similar to environment variables: **dev: lambdaFunction=my-api-dev**; **prod: lambdaFunction=my-api-prod**. An integration can interpolate the function name or alias. A variable selects a target; it grants no invocation permission.

**Incoming authorisation:** IAM uses signed requests (normally SigV4), Cognito User Pools validate configured user tokens/scopes, and Lambda authorisers run custom logic. HTTP APIs also support native JWT authorisers. **STS is not a standalone API Gateway authoriser**: a trusted caller may AssumeRole, receive temporary credentials, then sign an AWS_IAM API request.

For the backend hop, use a Lambda resource-policy Allow for **apigateway.amazonaws.com**, scoped by the appropriate **execute-api source ARN** and selected function/alias. Alternatively configure API Gateway to assume a trusted invocation role with lambda:InvokeFunction permission. Console-created integrations may add Lambda permission automatically; stage-variable targets still need matching grants.
learning.analogy: The caller shows a ticket; the receptionist needs permission to call the office; the office worker needs permission to open the filing cabinet. Changing the office number grants none of those permissions.

rows: IAM/SigV4, Cognito or Lambda authoriser as configured
Invoke the API method; STS only supplies credentials for the IAM path
Function resource policy OR configured IAM invocation role
Required DynamoDB actions on the table/index

learning.example:
# Integration target shorthand (not a complete ARN)
${stageVariables.lambdaFunction}

# Executable permission shape; substitute your IDs and target
aws lambda add-permission --function-name my-api-dev \
  --statement-id apigw-dev-get-order --action lambda:InvokeFunction \
  --principal apigateway.amazonaws.com \
  --source-arn 'arn:aws:execute-api:ap-southeast-2:111111111111:API_ID/dev/GET/GetOrder'
# For a qualified alias target, scope permission to the matching alias.
learning.trigger: API accepted caller but returns 500 before Lambda runs → inspect integration target and invoke permission. Lambda AccessDenied downstream → execution role.
learning.trap: A Lambda execution role controls outgoing AWS calls, not who may invoke the function. For the alternative role path, both trust and permissions must be correct; explicit Deny still applies.

lambda.name: AWS Lambda
lambda.role: Execute event-driven code without operating a conventional server fleet.
bullets: For conventional Lambda compute, memory is 128–10,240 MB; CPU grows with memory, with about one vCPU at 1,769 MB.
Layers share code/dependencies and custom runtime content; they do not allocate extra CPU.
Published versions are immutable. $LATEST is unpublished. An alias points to a published version and can weight a second version.
lambda.boundary: Call the alias to use its routing policy. An alias cannot point to another alias. A new version alone does not create a canary.

rows: Independent CPU selector for this compute mode

lambda.note: Rollback: remove additional weights and route prod to v1. Measure duration and cost together. Lambda Managed Instances has different compute configuration; do not generalize this memory-only rule to every Lambda offering.

learning.title: Scaling: cold start vs concurrency vs CPU
paragraphs: On-demand Lambda automatically adds execution environments within scaling/concurrency quotas. Reserved concurrency reserves AND caps a function’s concurrency; it does not warm environments. Provisioned concurrency pre-initialises environments on a version/alias; excess requests can use on-demand capacity when allowed.

Application Auto Scaling can schedule provisioned concurrency before a known peak or target-track provisioned-concurrency utilisation for variable load. Scheduling is proactive; target tracking reacts and needs time to scale.

Cold-start latency → consider provisioned concurrency after measuring initialisation. CPU-heavy handler duration → increase memory (128–10,240 MB for standard functions; ~1 vCPU at 1,769 MB), profile and measure cost/duration. Warm environments do not supply extra per-invocation CPU.
learning.trap: Reserved concurrency is not provisioned concurrency; neither a layer nor a warm environment fixes CPU starvation.

learning.title: Invocation errors: who owns retry and the DLQ?

rows: Caller waits for result/error; caller or invoking service owns retry
Function error can be in a successful Invoke API response; inspect FunctionError/payload
Lambda queue; default 2 retries for function errors
Throttle/system errors retry with backoff up to the event-age window (6 h default); duplicates possible
Configure Lambda DLQ (SQS/SNS) or supported on-failure destination
DLQ stores failed event; destination adds invocation context; delivery also needs permissions
Lambda polls queue and deletes successful work
Use source queue redrive/DLQ; Lambda async-invocation DLQ is not this path

learning.trap: A queue-triggered Lambda is not the same as InvocationType=Event.

learning.title: Container/runtime and configuration contract
paragraphs: Lambda container images must be **Linux**, target **one architecture** (x86_64 or arm64), and stay within **10 GB uncompressed including layers**. Multi-architecture images are not supported; a normal container image still needs Lambda-compatible invocation handling.

**Runtime API** is the HTTP contract to fetch invocations/report results. A **Runtime Interface Client (RIC)** implements that contract inside the image/runtime. The **Runtime Interface Emulator (RIE)** is a local testing proxy; it does not emulate IAM, AWS networking or all service behaviour.

Environment variables are strings with an aggregate **4 KB** limit for a function. Store large configuration externally; use Secrets Manager/Parameter Store when appropriate rather than treating env vars as a secret-rotation system.
learning.trigger: CPU-intensive code → tune memory; large container dependencies → image packaging, still subject to Lambda quotas.

learning.title: Node.js ZIP: declaring a dependency does not install it
paragraphs: **package.json** declares packages; **node_modules/** contains their installed code. Lambda does not run npm install when you upload a ZIP. Install/build in development or CI, then ship the handler at the archive root with required dependencies. With an existing lockfile, npm ci provides a reproducible install.

A layer can provide dependencies separately (Node.js layers use the supported nodejs/node_modules path); a container image is another packaging model. Bundle the runtime/library versions you require explicitly, even when the runtime includes an SDK. Native modules must match the Lambda Linux runtime and architecture.
learning.analogy: A shopping list is not a pantry. Ship the ingredients, not only the list.

rows: npm install to update lockfile; npm ci --omit=dev in CI
Package index.js and installed production dependencies
Handler executes; no automatic npm install
Configure permissions, secrets and connectivity separately
Driver connects to PostgreSQL; packaging does not create the database

learning.trigger: Cannot find module pg after ZIP upload → verify installed dependency files/layer and archive paths, not just package.json.
learning.trap: npm ci needs a matching lockfile. Bundlers/layers can change the artifact shape, but required runtime code must still be present.

cfn.name: AWS CloudFormation
cfn.role: Provision related resources as a versioned stack.
bullets: Resources is required. Parameters, Mappings, Conditions, Outputs and Transform are optional sections.
DependsOn is a resource attribute; there is no top-level Dependencies section. Ref/GetAtt also create implicit dependencies.
Conditions gate resources/outputs or property values through Fn::If. Parameters supply inputs; a Condition cannot be attached to a parameter.
cfn.boundary: Export names are unique per account/Region. Standard Fn::ImportValue references stay in that account/Region; an active import prevents changing/deleting the exported value.
cfn.example:
AWSTemplateFormatVersion: '2010-09-09'
Parameters:
  Environment:
    Type: String
    AllowedValues: [dev, prod]
Conditions:
  IsProd: !Equals [!Ref Environment, prod]
Resources:
  Orders:
    Type: AWS::SQS::Queue
    Properties:
      MessageRetentionPeriod: !If [IsProd, 1209600, 345600]
Outputs:
  QueueArn:
    Value: !GetAtt Orders.Arn
    Export:
      Name: !Sub '${AWS::StackName}-QueueArn'

rows: Parameter value or resource-specific return value

cfn.note: StackSets deploy a template across selected accounts/Regions with parameters and permissions. This is different from a same-Region export/import dependency. Consult current docs for newer cross-Region output-reference features.

learning.title: Valid parameters, Conditions vs DependsOn
paragraphs: Parameter types include **String, Number, List<Number>, CommaDelimitedList**, supported **AWS-specific types** (for example AWS::EC2::VPC::Id and List<AWS::EC2::Subnet::Id>), and supported **SSM parameter value types**. `DependentParameter` is not a valid type; native Boolean is not a parameter type either.

**Conditions** decide whether a resource/output is created or select a property through Fn::If. **DependsOn** controls ordering for resources that are created. It does not test an input or make a resource optional. References can create implicit dependencies.
learning.example:
Parameters:
  Stage:
    Type: String
    AllowedValues: [dev, prod]
Conditions:
  IsProd: !Equals [!Ref Stage, prod]
# Resource: Condition: IsProd → create only in prod.
# Resource: DependsOn: OtherResource → order, not a boolean check.

learning.title: Pseudo parameters: AWS supplies deployment context
paragraphs: Think of a template as a function: **Parameters** are user inputs; **pseudo parameters** are AWS-provided context. CloudFormation resolves references during stack deployment/evaluation, not as ordinary application compile-time constants.

**CDK synthesis** emits a CloudFormation template. Environment-aware CDK code can resolve some context earlier, but unresolved AWS references remain tokens for CloudFormation to resolve at deployment.
learning.analogy: The form asks you for a name; the office supplies its address and the assigned case number.
learning.flow: CDK code → synth template → CloudFormation deploy → resolve account/Region/stack context.

rows: ARN partition: aws, aws-cn, aws-us-gov, etc.
Remove a property when returned by Fn::If

learning.example:
# CloudFormation YAML excerpt
Outputs:
  Region:
    Value: !Ref AWS::Region
  Account:
    Value: !Ref AWS::AccountId
  Stack:
    Value: !Ref AWS::StackId
# Optional property pattern: !If [UseValue, value, !Ref AWS::NoValue]
learning.trigger: Need current account/Region without user input → pseudo parameter.
learning.trap: AWS::NoValue removes a property through Fn::If; it is not an empty string or a parameter you declare.

cdk.name: AWS CDK
cdk.role: Define AWS infrastructure using programming-language constructs.
bullets: Compose constructs into stacks/apps using TypeScript, JavaScript, Python, Java, C#/.NET or Go.
cdk synth produces CloudFormation templates; cdk deploy uses CloudFormation to create or update the stack.
Covers serverless and other infrastructure: Lambda, APIs, VPCs, EC2, ECS, databases and more. Reusable constructs can generate many resources.
cdk.boundary: CDK is not a runtime and is not limited to servers. SAM and CDK both describe infrastructure; choose serverless YAML shorthand/local tooling versus general programming-language composition.
cdk.example:
from aws_cdk import Stack, aws_lambda as lambda_
from constructs import Construct

class OrdersStack(Stack):
    def __init__(self, scope: Construct, construct_id: str, **kwargs):
        super().__init__(scope, construct_id, **kwargs)
        lambda_.Function(self, "Orders",
            runtime=lambda_.Runtime.PYTHON_3_13,
            handler="app.handler",
            code=lambda_.Code.from_asset("src"))

rows: Deployment unit that maps to a CloudFormation stack
Generate CloudFormation; does not start a production application

cdk.exampleTitle: CDK stack excerpt · creates a Lambda function
cdk.note: cdk init → write constructs → build if needed → cdk synth → cdk deploy. SAM can also declare ordinary CloudFormation resources; serverless scope versus broad infrastructure is a preference, not an absolute capability boundary.

learning.title: diff previews; deploy changes resources
paragraphs: `cdk diff` compares the synthesised stack with its deployed state and displays proposed differences; it does not apply the application update. Its default workflow may use a temporary CloudFormation change set for replacement accuracy.
`cdk deploy` provisions/updates through CloudFormation. Neither command runs your business application locally; the provisioned Lambda/EC2/ECS resources execute it.
learning.trigger: Review proposed infrastructure changes → diff; apply reviewed changes → deploy.

sam.name: AWS SAM
sam.role: Define, build, test and deploy a serverless application.
bullets: The SAM template extends CloudFormation; Transform: AWS::Serverless-2016-10-31 expands shorthand into deployable resources.
The SAM CLI builds/packages code, invokes supported functions locally, emulates supported API routes and deploys through CloudFormation.
Mix AWS::Serverless::* shorthand with standard AWS::* resources in the same template. The resulting Lambda functions/API/database run in AWS.
sam.boundary: SAM is infrastructure and development tooling, not compute. AWS::Serverless::UserPool is invalid; use AWS::Cognito::UserPool. Local testing does not reproduce every cloud behavior.
sam.example:
Transform: AWS::Serverless-2016-10-31
Resources:
  Handler:
    Type: AWS::Serverless::Function
    Properties:
      Runtime: python3.13
      Handler: app.handler
      CodeUri: src/
      Events:
        GetOrder:
          Type: HttpApi
          Properties:
            Path: /GetOrder
            Method: GET
  Users:
    Type: AWS::Cognito::UserPool

rows: Lambda function + supported events, permissions and deployment settings
A DynamoDB table with simplified configuration
Nested/reusable serverless application, including SAR applications

sam.exampleTitle: SAM template excerpt · HTTP API + Lambda + standard Cognito resource
sam.note: sam init → sam build → sam local invoke / sam local start-api → sam deploy --guided. The table lists common types; the current reference includes additional shorthand resources. SAM remains explicit in exam skills 3.2.4, 3.3.1, 3.3.4 and 3.4.3.

learning.title: sam sync vs sam deploy: feedback loop vs managed release

rows: Fast development loop; supported code updates use service APIs directly; other changes can use CloudFormation
Do not assume a stack rollback reverses direct code syncs
Normal stack failure/rollback behaviour unless explicitly disabled; use versioned artifacts for release
Repeatable stack deployment + tested versions/aliases/hooks as appropriate
Use sync in a development stack, not as a replacement for controlled promotion

learning.trap: sam sync is not exclusively API-only: unsupported/code-independent infrastructure changes can trigger a CloudFormation deployment.

sar.name: AWS Serverless Application Repository
sar.role: Find, share and deploy versioned reusable serverless applications.
bullets: Applications package a SAM template with deployment artifacts; choose an application version and supply its parameters.
Publish privately for a team/organization or publicly, subject to sharing permissions.
AWS::Serverless::Application can reference a repository application; deployment creates the underlying application resources.
sar.boundary: SAR is an application repository, not compute. Service Catalog governs approved products; AWS Marketplace distributes third-party software/services.
sar.example:
Transform: AWS::Serverless-2016-10-31
Resources:
  SharedApplication:
    Type: AWS::Serverless::Application
    Properties:
      Location:
        ApplicationId: arn:aws:serverlessrepo:us-east-1:123456789012:applications/example-app
        SemanticVersion: 1.0.0
sar.exampleTitle: Reference a SAR application · illustrative ARN/version
sar.note: Replace the application ARN/version, grant required access and provide the application’s required parameters. Inspect the template and permissions before deployment.

dynamodb.name: Amazon DynamoDB
dynamodb.role: Key-value/document storage organized around key-based access.
bullets: GameName + Version identifies a game version; querying GameName returns its versions. Category + GameName on a GSI supports category lookup.
A GSI only returns projected attributes; use ALL when the index must return every game attribute. GSI reads are eventually consistent.
TTL is a Number containing Unix seconds. Expiration is asynchronous cleanup; TTL deletions can appear in Streams. Filter expired data when required.
dynamodb.boundary: Read-then-write can race. Use an atomic conditional write for a request ID, then coordinate status/results with business side effects.

learning.title: Capacity, hot partitions and scaling
paragraphs: **Provisioned capacity** is the configured budget; **Auto Scaling** changes that budget in response to utilisation, with reaction time. **Adaptive capacity** reallocates available capacity towards unevenly accessed partitions; it cannot create unlimited table/partition capacity or rescue every single hot key.

Distribute high-volume access across partition keys. Adding total WCU/RCU or switching to on-demand is not a universal cure for a hot item. For a voucher, condition the owner/balance update and use a transaction across ownership items.
learning.trigger: Hot key despite available table capacity → inspect key distribution and per-partition pressure, not only total WCU.

learning.title: Read/write capacity: round size, then apply the rate
paragraphs: **Strong** reads return the latest successfully committed data; **eventual** reads can be stale and consume half the read capacity, not two reads. The calculator models successful single-item reads/writes of equally sized items; KB here means 1,024 bytes, including attribute names and values.

**12 KB × 16 eventual reads/s:** ceil(12/4) = 3 size units; 3 × 0.5 = 1.5 units/read; 1.5 × 16 = **24 RCUs**. Consumed units describe operations; provisioned units describe throughput per second. On-demand uses analogous request-unit arithmetic rather than provisioned RCU/WCU settings.
learning.analogy: Buy capacity in rounded cartons: a partly filled carton still costs one carton; read consistency changes its price.
learning.flow: Item bytes → round to 4 KB read / 1 KB write units → consistency/transaction multiplier → requests per second.

rows: 1 write unit per 1 KB, rounded up
1 read unit per 4 KB, rounded up
0.5 read unit per 4 KB, rounded up
2 read units per 4 KB, rounded up
2 write units per 1 KB, rounded up

learning.trigger: Round item size before multiplying by request rate; transactions cost twice the equivalent strong-read/normal-write capacity.
learning.trap: This single-item formula is not a universal Query/Scan estimator. Index writes, updates, condition failures and actual access distribution can add considerations; provision headroom.

learning.title: LSI vs GSI: another access path, not a reordered table
paragraphs: Like a relational index, an index offers a different lookup order. It does **not** physically reorder the original table. An LSI is not necessarily a simple pointer: it stores index keys and projected attributes. “Local” refers to sharing the table partition key and related storage organisation; GSI storage/partitioning is separate.

The **10 GB LSI item-collection limit** applies per partition-key value to the base-table items plus their LSI entries. Creating LSIs only with the table is a DynamoDB design constraint, not a rule for all databases. A newly added GSI backfills existing eligible items before becoming active.

**Provisioned accounting:** LSI reads/writes share the table budget. GSI queries use the index’s eventual-read RCUs, not table RCUs. Writes to eligible base items can also write index entries; their sizes/changed keys determine the extra WCUs. Insufficient GSI write capacity can back-pressure base writes. Separate index reads, writes and storage add cost, but a suitable GSI can replace expensive repeated scans.
learning.analogy: Two library catalogues: LSI keeps the same reader’s drawer with a new sort order; GSI provides a separate set of drawers by another key.
learning.flow: Orders base UserID + OrderID → LSI UserID + OrderDate; GSI OrderStatus + OrderDate.

Can use different partition and sort keys

learning.trap: Global means a different table-wide access path, not a cross-Region index.

learning.title: Query vs Scan vs Parallel Scan
paragraphs: **CLI view:** projection chooses attributes (columns); filtering chooses returned items (rows), after reads. For the same evaluated data, neither reduces Scan capacity. CLI output pagination is separate from DynamoDB’s service-level LastEvaluatedKey/ExclusiveStartKey. Use the playground above for both Users and a 250-object S3 listing.
learning.analogy: Query goes to the right filing drawer; Scan checks every drawer; Parallel Scan gives several clerks different portions of the filing room.
learning.flow: Suitable table/index partition key → Query. Otherwise Scan → process page → follow LastEvaluatedKey; parallel workers scan separate logical segments.

rows: An existing suitable table/index key may already suffice
Evaluate table/index items, up to 1 MB per page
FilterExpression and ProjectionExpression do not reduce Scan read capacity

Can reduce elapsed time, but increases simultaneous read pressure

# Pseudocode: four concurrent workers; each paginates independently
def worker(segment):
    start = None
    while True:
        page = scan(TableName="Orders", Segment=segment,
                    TotalSegments=4, ExclusiveStartKey=start) # omit key initially
        process(page["Items"])
        start = page.get("LastEvaluatedKey")
        if not start: break
run_concurrently(worker, segments=range(4))

aws dynamodb scan --table-name Users \
  --projection-expression "UserID, #n" \
  --filter-expression "#a = :yes" \
  --expression-attribute-names '{"#n":"Name","#a":"Active"}' \
  --expression-attribute-values '{":yes":{"BOOL":true}}' \
  --page-size 4 --max-items 5
# Resume using the returned CLI NextToken: --starting-token "TOKEN"

learning.trap: A filter runs after reads. Segments are logical scan work, not a promise of one worker per physical partition; pagination still applies.

learning.title: DAX vs Redis vs CloudFront: cache the right boundary
paragraphs: **DAX** shares eligible DynamoDB item/query results across clients; it is not a separate cache per signed-in user. Reuse depends on keys and query inputs. A DAX-compatible SDK/client and cluster endpoint handle lookup, population and much of the cache lifecycle. Cache hits are eventually consistent; strong reads pass through to DynamoDB and do not populate the cache.

**Redis can cache DynamoDB data.** Your application controls lookup, miss handling, population, TTL and invalidation. Choose it for custom keys, session data or computed values. For static S3 images, use **CloudFront** in the HTTP delivery path. Always preserve authorisation/tenant scope; a shared cache is not an entitlement check.
learning.analogy: DAX is a DynamoDB-aware librarian; Redis is a general-purpose shelf you organise; CloudFront is a worldwide HTTP delivery depot.

Browser → edge cache → HTTP origin such as S3
Static assets and appropriate cacheable HTTP responses
Latest successfully committed data; a GSI cannot serve strong reads

learning.trigger: Repeated DynamoDB products + least cache logic → DAX. Arbitrary sessions/computation → Redis. S3 images → CloudFront.
learning.trap: DAX does not provide strong cache hits; it can forward strong reads. Redis is capable of caching DynamoDB, but is not a direct CDN replacement.

sqs.name: Amazon SQS
sqs.role: Buffer work so consumers can process it independently.
bullets: Receive hides a message; DeleteMessage acknowledges success. Default visibility is 30 seconds, maximum 12 hours; duplicates still require idempotency.
PurgeQueue removes messages and keeps the queue. DeleteQueue removes both. RemovePermission edits queue-policy permission.
Choose queue type at creation; it cannot be converted later. Source and DLQ types must match. Queue tags are case-sensitive.
sqs.boundary: VisibilityTimeout hides received work; DelaySeconds postpones initial availability; MessageRetentionPeriod limits retention. They are different clocks.

rows: Ordered within a message group; producer deduplication

sqs.note: Backlog per worker = ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible / running workers. Target backlog = acceptable wait / average processing time. Apply target tracking to ECS with an appropriate task-count metric and a scale-from-zero strategy.

learning.title: Polling, in-flight messages and large payloads
paragraphs: Stored messages are waiting in the queue; **in-flight** messages have been received but not deleted. Standard queues have an approximately **120,000** in-flight limit depending on traffic/backlog; FIFO currently supports **120,000**. There is no fixed count quota on stored backlog, but retention and service quotas still apply.

**Short polling** (WaitTimeSeconds=0) samples servers and may return false-empty results. **Long polling** (1–20 s) queries all servers and waits for messages, reducing empty responses. At the Standard in-flight limit, short polling can return OverLimit; long polling waits without returning more messages until slots free.

Native messages are now up to **1 MiB (1,048,576 bytes)**, not the older 256 KB. The Java/Python **SQS Extended Client** stores large payloads in S3 (up to 2 GB) and queues a reference. Consumers need S3 permissions and coordinated object cleanup; this is not a native multi-GB queue body.

Visibility is a processing lease, not deletion. For Lambda polling SQS, configure the source queue redrive policy/DLQ. Lambda async-invocation retry/DLQ settings apply to its separate asynchronous queue, not SQS event source mappings.
learning.trigger: Excess empty receives → long polling; repeated processing → inspect visibility, failures and idempotency.
learning.trap: Increasing stored backlog is not identical to hitting the in-flight limit.

learning.title: Message encryption: service-side vs client-side
paragraphs: SSE-KMS uses [envelope encryption](#cryptography): SQS manages data-key use, not the producer’s application logic. Producers generally need **kms:GenerateDataKey + kms:Decrypt**; consumers need **kms:Decrypt** for relevant keys. Check the key policy and service integrations too.
See [IAM identity vs queue policies](#dva-service-iam) for who may call SendMessage/ReceiveMessage. Secrets Manager stores secrets; it is not the service encrypting queue storage.
learning.analogy: The queue locks its storage room for you; client-side encryption puts a separately locked box inside that room.
learning.flow: Authorised producer → TLS → SQS encrypts message body at rest → SQS decrypts → authorised consumer over TLS.

rows: Transparent service encryption; no KMS key permissions
Usually unchanged Send/Receive code; check IAM and KMS permissions
Requires encrypt/decrypt code and its own key-access model

learning.trigger: Encrypt SQS messages at rest with KMS and minimal application change → SSE-KMS with appropriate permissions.
learning.trap: SSE does not mean the consumer must implement local decryption. Client-side encryption can add confidentiality but changes the application.

learning.title: FIFO: group orders work; deduplication identifies a send
paragraphs: The five-minute deduplication history can outlive receiving/deleting the original message. Suppression does not delete an already queued message, and a retry outside the window can enqueue again. FIFO ordering and send deduplication do not make business side effects exactly once: visibility expiry, failures and retries still require application idempotency.
learning.analogy: MessageGroupId chooses the checkout lane; MessageDeduplicationId is the receipt number that identifies one logical purchase.

learning.trap: A new random ID on every retry defeats explicit send deduplication. Same body with different attributes still hashes identically in content-based mode.

kinesis.name: Kinesis Data Streams
kinesis.role: Retain continuous events in shard lanes for independent, replayable reads.
bullets: A stream contains shards; shards contain records. Partition keys map records to a shard, where Kinesis assigns sequence numbers.
PutRecords batches records. HTTP 200 can include partial failures: inspect FailedRecordCount and each result; retry only failed entries with backoff and jitter.
ProvisionedThroughputExceededException indicates capacity/hot-key pressure; InternalFailure is a service-side record error. Preserve an application event ID for deduplication.
kinesis.boundary: Spreading partition keys can fix a hot shard. Increasing provisioned shards can add capacity; merging shards or sending more requests does not fix producer throttling.

rows: Scaling boundaries, hot keys and quotas still apply

kinesis.exampleTitle: PutRecords response: retry the second input record
kinesis.note: Results align with request order. PutRecords does not guarantee ordering across successful and retried records. Reducing readers does not directly fix producer-side write throttling.

learning.title: Shard budgets, hot keys and read contention
paragraphs: For sustained **provisioned** writes, each shard has up to **1 MiB/s and 1,000 records/s**. Ten evenly used shards provide up to 10 MiB/s aggregate byte throughput. Spare capacity on other shards is not a common pool for a hot shard.

A partition key hashes to one shard. Many well-spread keys can exploit additional/split shards; a single hot key still stays together. Reducing shard count cannot solve hot-key pressure. Retry only failed PutRecords entries with exponential backoff and jitter, then address capacity/key distribution.

Shared consumers share **2 MiB/s and 5 GetRecords calls/s per shard**; enhanced fan-out gives each registered consumer up to **2 MiB/s per shard**. This isolates read throughput, not producer write pressure or slow processing. Reads do not delete records: **24 h default retention**, extendable to **365 days**, enables replay with independent consumer positions.
learning.trigger: Low aggregate utilisation + one saturated shard → partition-key skew. Shared consumer read contention → enhanced fan-out, not more producer retries.
learning.trap: Shard-count quotas vary by Region/account and can change; LimitExceededException does not inherently mean “one shard is full”.
learning.analogy: Ten checkout lanes do not help if every customer queues at lane one.
learning.flow: Producer partition key → hash range → one shard’s write budget; consumers later share/read that shard’s separate read budget.

rows: Write shard/record rate or shared read pressure; inspect the failing operation
Account/Region quota or API-operation limit; inspect the API/error context

learning.title: Streams vs delivery vs continuous analytics
paragraphs: ElastiCache, DynamoDB and RDS are **not native Firehose destination types**. To write there, build a suitable consumer/custom integration with its own retries, throughput and transaction handling; an arbitrary HTTP endpoint does not make them native destinations.

rows: Retained log with producers, shard lanes and independent consumers
Replay/event processing; consumers own read progress
Buffered managed delivery to a configured destination
S3, Redshift (stage in S3 then COPY), OpenSearch, Splunk, Iceberg and supported HTTP/partner destinations
Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink
Stateful streaming computation, windows, joins and aggregations

learning.trigger: Deliver buffered records to S3 with minimal consumer code → Firehose. Compute continuous windowed analytics → Flink. Independent retained replay → Data Streams.

learning.title: KCL workers: shard leases are the unit of ownership
paragraphs: Within **one consumer application**, KCL assigns each shard lease to one active worker in steady state. One worker can run record processors for several shards. With **10 shards and 20 one-worker EC2 instances**, at most 10 workers perform shard-level work concurrently in this simplified model; the rest cannot create extra shard parallelism.

Separate application identities have independent lease/checkpoint sets and can each consume the stream. This does not create more stream write capacity; shared-read throughput or enhanced fan-out limits still apply. Lease recovery and checkpoints do not eliminate duplicate processing after failures.
learning.analogy: A worker holds the checkout-lane assignment; one worker can cover several lanes, but twenty workers cannot invent twenty lanes in a ten-lane store.
learning.trigger: More EC2 consumers than shards in one KCL app → no extra shard-level parallelism. Independent apps are a different boundary.
learning.trap: A shard lease is not a shard copied to a worker. This is steady-state assignment, not an exactly-once side-effect guarantee.

containers.name: Amazon ECS
containers.role: Orchestrate container tasks and services; choose their compute separately.
bullets: ECS schedules tasks/services. A task definition is the container blueprint; a service maintains the desired tasks. EC2 and Fargate are distinct capacity choices.
Task-local ephemeral/bind-mount data is suitable for temporary files. EC2 host volumes depend on host lifecycle.
EFS provides persistent shared network files for supported ECS/Fargate tasks across AZs. Configure mount targets, NFS access and file permissions.
containers.boundary: A local volume is not a shared cross-AZ filesystem. Fargate EFS support requires a supported Linux platform; do not assume every OS/launch mode supports it.
containers.note: The excerpt omits task roles, CPU/memory, networking and other required task settings. Add an EFS access point/IAM authorization where needed; a mount declaration alone does not grant access.

learning.title: ECS container instance registration vs EC2 lifecycle
paragraphs: For **ECS on EC2**, the ECS agent registers a container instance with the cluster. Drain it before planned termination to stop placing tasks and replace service tasks appropriately.

Terminating a running EC2 container instance with a connected agent normally deregisters it automatically. Stopped instances or disconnected agents can leave stale registrations requiring manual deregistration.

Deregistering an ECS container instance does not terminate the EC2 instance or stop its billing. Forced deregistration can orphan running tasks. These are EC2 host concerns, not a Fargate host-management procedure.
learning.trap: The ECS cluster inventory and the underlying billable EC2 fleet are separate resources.

fargate.name: AWS Fargate
fargate.role: Supply managed compute capacity for containers without managing EC2 hosts.
bullets: For ECS, define the image, task CPU/memory, networking and roles; Fargate supplies isolated task compute.
ECS still schedules tasks/services. You continue to own the container, IAM permissions, security groups and application behavior.
Task-local storage is ephemeral. Use supported EFS integration when tasks need shared persistent files.
fargate.boundary: Fargate is container compute; ECS is orchestration. Fargate does not build images or define infrastructure templates. Choose self-managed EC2 capacity when host-level requirements demand it.

rows: Managed task compute; supported CPU/memory/platform combinations
Discounted interruptible capacity; design interruption-tolerant work

fargate.note: Add task execution/application roles and the network configuration when launching tasks. The task execution role covers supported agent actions such as image pulls; the task role grants permissions to application code.

rds.name: Amazon RDS
rds.role: Managed relational databases with SQL and transactions.
bullets: Read replicas asynchronously copy data; the application must send reads to replica endpoints. Expect possible replication lag.
A traditional Multi-AZ DB instance has a standby for failover, not reads.
A Multi-AZ DB cluster has readable standby DB instances; engine/configuration support matters.
rds.boundary: Read load points to replicas; failover points to Multi-AZ; repeated reusable results may point to a cache. These choices can coexist.
rds.example:
# Application routing, not an AWS API payload
write_connection = connect(primary_endpoint)
report_connection = connect(read_replica_endpoint)
# Use the primary for reads that require the latest committed value.

learning.title: SQL transactions, OLTP and OLAP
paragraphs: With **RDS MySQL / InnoDB**, wrap a voucher/game purchase in START TRANSACTION → debit / create entitlement with correct locking or conditions → COMMIT. On failure, ROLLBACK the transaction explicitly as appropriate; do not assume every SQL error aborts the entire transaction. Autocommit on separate statements does not make them one atomic bundle.

**OLTP** serves many short operational reads/writes (orders, balances); **OLAP** scans/aggregates historical datasets for analytics (for example a Redshift warehouse). SQL is used in both; a read replica scales reads but does not turn every OLTP schema into an analytics warehouse.

learning.title: Automated backups vs long-term snapshots
paragraphs: RDS DB-instance automated-backup retention is **0–35 days** (0 disables it); Multi-AZ DB clusters use **1–35 days**. Creation defaults differ: CLI/API DB instance default 1 day, console default 7 days. Point-in-time recovery creates a new database resource.

**Manual snapshots** persist until explicitly deleted. For longer-term policy-based retention, use manual snapshots or an appropriate **AWS Backup** plan. Replicas and Multi-AZ are not a backup retention policy.

For a custom periodic DB-instance snapshot workflow: **EventBridge Scheduler → Lambda → CreateDBSnapshot** with execution permissions and unique names. Scheduler can also call supported AWS APIs directly; Lambda is useful when custom naming/retention logic is needed. Define cleanup, idempotency and snapshot-quota handling.
learning.trigger: Retain backups beyond the automated retention window → snapshots/AWS Backup, not an oversized BackupRetentionPeriod.

cache.name: Amazon ElastiCache
cache.role: Keep frequently reused data in memory.
bullets: Valkey, Redis OSS and Memcached support low-latency cached access; choose engine capabilities deliberately.
A cache hit can reduce database work. A miss still needs a source-of-truth lookup.
Use expiry and invalidation to manage staleness. Memcached is not a durable primary database.
cache.boundary: A cache endpoint does not execute relational SQL in place of RDS. Cache-aside requires application logic and a key design.

rows: Provisioned nodes; reservation options where supported

learning.title: Redis/Valkey vs Memcached: replicas, failover and shards
paragraphs: Read-heavy repeated database results and expensive computed values (rendered pages, recommendations, aggregations) can both benefit from caching. Key by the actual inputs and set invalidation/TTL; non-reusable CPU work is not accelerated merely by adding a cache.

This engine/topology comparison describes node-based clusters. ElastiCache Serverless manages availability across AZs itself; do not generalise node-based Memcached failure behaviour to its serverless offering. The standard cache-node topology below excludes the newer Valkey 9.0+ durability mode, which uses a Multi-AZ transactional log and has different write/recovery guarantees.

A **node** is one running cache server; a **shard** owns a subset of the keyspace; a node-based Redis replication group/cluster contains one or more shards. Cluster mode disabled has **one shard**; enabled supports multiple. Each shard has one primary and **optional** replicas. Redis Cluster maps keys to **16,384 hash slots**.

**Asynchronous replication** copies each primary’s data to its replicas in both modes. Replicas increase read capacity and provide promotion candidates, not additional writers. Shards scale aggregate writes/storage. Enable automatic failover/Multi-AZ with an appropriate replica topology for availability; replication can lose recent writes during failure.
Both node-based Redis OSS/Valkey and Memcached clusters are **regional**; nodes can span AZs. More nodes is not cross-Region deployment. A hot single key still maps to one shard.
For the DynamoDB-native cache vs general-purpose cache vs CDN choice, use the [DAX/Redis/CloudFront comparison](#dva-service-dynamodb).

rows: Rich data types, replication and supported persistence/HA features
Replication group: primary writes, replicas read; Multi-AZ automatic failover promotes a replica
Multiple shards partition keyspace; each shard has its own primary and optional replicas
Sharding increases aggregate capacity; replicas/failover improve read/availability characteristics
Simple multithreaded distributed cache; client distributes keys across nodes
No Redis-style replication groups, automatic replica promotion or durable primary storage

learning.trigger: Need replication + automatic failover or rich structures → supported Redis/Valkey topology. Need disposable simple distributed cache → Memcached can fit.
learning.trap: A replica is not an extra write shard; a cache is not the relational SQL endpoint.
learning.analogy: Shards are different book collections; replicas are extra copies of the same collection. Extra copies let more people read, not write to a new collection.
learning.flow: Client hashes key → owning shard primary → asynchronous replica copy; read-capable clients can use replicas deliberately.

learning.title: Cache strategy: who updates the cached representation?
paragraphs: These are application patterns, not a Redis setting that makes database/cache writes atomic. Write-through **updates** the cached representation; write-invalidate **deletes** it after the database commit. Either write workflow can be synchronous or asynchronous; latency, ordering, failures and races still need design.

Exam examples: **popular profiles + limited cache + up to 60 s staleness** → lazy loading + TTL; **blog updates + fresher cached content** → write-through is the intended pattern; **product price updates without maintaining a cached representation** → database write then invalidate. Strict zero-staleness needs stronger consistency/concurrency controls than these basic patterns alone.
learning.analogy: Lazy loading fills a shelf when someone asks; TTL puts a use-by time on it; write-through replaces the shelf copy; invalidation removes the old copy.

rows: Miss fetches DB and populates cache; DB writes alone do not update cache
Only requested items cached; can remain stale until eviction/invalidation
Same miss path; entries expire after a chosen duration
Next read refreshes; expiry itself performs no DB fetch
DB write + cache set/update in the application workflow
Fresher on successful writes; can cache never-read data and adds write work
DB commit → delete cache key → next read repopulates
Avoids maintaining new cached value; failed delete/concurrent reads can still leave stale data

learning.trigger: Choose by freshness tolerance, read reuse and write workflow—not merely by engine name.
learning.trap: A TTL does not refresh automatically. Updating the DB and cache in two calls is not an atomic transaction.

iam.name: IAM, STS & Access Analyzer
iam.role: Establish AWS trust and evaluate permissions.
bullets: Identity policies grant actions; supported resource policies grant access to resources. A role trust policy says who may assume it; STS issues temporary credentials.
Permissions boundaries and SCPs limit applicable permissions; they do not grant actions. An explicit applicable deny overrides an allow.
Access Analyzer finds supported external/unused access and validates policies. Policy variables can scope reusable access, e.g. an IAM user’s own S3 prefix.
iam.boundary: Trusting an identity does not authorize every resource. ${aws:username} is for IAM users and is not generally present for role sessions; use suitable principal tags/identity variables.
iam.note: Billing-console access can require the account root user to Activate IAM Access plus appropriate IAM permissions. SCPs govern member-account principals within their documented scope; they are not a universal policy attached to every possible caller.

learning.title: Identity policy vs SQS queue policy
learning.analogy: An identity policy is an employee’s badge; a queue policy is the guest list on the room. A role trust policy controls who can borrow a badge.
learning.flow: Lambda uses its execution role → sqs:SendMessage → SQS evaluates applicable identity/queue policies. There is no special “SQS role”.

Lambda execution role allows sqs:SendMessage on Orders

Typically requires both identity-side and queue-side Allows
